title: Your family's story
hook: every Sikh family carries part of this history

segments.voice: Yesterday, chardi kala, and your line was the lesson of the story. Today the long story comes home, to an older voice and one question.

Where were you when you were my age? A boy asks it in the car on the way home from the gurdwara, mostly to fill the quiet. His grandfather, in the passenger seat, doesn't answer right away. Then he says the name of a village the boy has never heard. A well at the edge of it. A school two fields away. A morning when everyone packed what they could carry. The car pulls into the driveway, the engine stops, and nobody reaches for the door.
screen: `WHERE WERE YOU AT MY AGE?` → `A VILLAGE HE'S NEVER HEARD OF.` → `NOBODY REACHES FOR THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The big story lives in small ones. This year the path followed Gurus, marches, borders and ships, but the history doesn't sit only in books. Sikh families carry pieces of it: who crossed which border, who left a village, who drove a taxi through a first winter, who kept the Granth safe in a spare room. A family story is the long story at the size of one table. Sikhs pass on the Gurus' own lives as sakhis, stories told aloud, often by elders to children. The family story belongs to that same habit: the past handed over by voice. In the Japji, at the opening Angs of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak gives a run of short verses to suniai, listening. Each says what listening does: through listening, sorrow and wrongdoing are wiped away, and the devotees bloom. In Sikh practice, listening isn't only being polite. It's spiritual work. And how to ask? Some memories are sweet, and some hurt. A grandparent may laugh about a first job and go quiet about a border. So ask gently, one thing at a time, and let them decide how far to go. If they say no, that's an answer too. If they say yes, write it down, or ask to record it, because a story that lives in one voice can be lost. Elders are the archive no one else has.
screen: `THE LONG STORY AT ONE TABLE.` · `SAKHIS: STORIES TOLD ALOUD.` · `SUNIAI: LISTENING AS SPIRITUAL WORK.` · `ASK GENTLY, ONE THING AT A TIME.` · then, large: `ASK YOUR ELDERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind an elder, a grandparent, a parent, an old neighbor, a teacher, someone at the gurdwara or a place of worship you know, and picture their hands. Breathe in and wonder what those hands have done that you've never heard about; breathe out and let one question form, the one you'd most like to ask, and just find it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Sakhi. A story of the Gurus' lives told aloud, the way families also pass on their own long history by voice, kept by those who stop to listen. Today's word.
Your line: ask your elders. The car is still sitting in the driveway. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1045 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOUR PLACE IN THE STORY.`
